meta.subtitle: Q2 revenue +21%, EPS +43%, client assets $13.08T; FY25 borrowings below cash. BUY by a narrow margin, decided by the Base multiple.

analystCommentary: We rate Schwab BUY with a $113-$128 target range, and the call sits close to the line between BUY and HOLD. The 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 shows the franchise compounding: total client assets reached $13.08 trillion, up 22% year-over-year, core net new assets were $119.8 billion, up 49%, and total net revenues rose 21% to $7.1 billion while total expenses excluding interest rose 12%. Diluted EPS was $1.54, up 43%, and return on tangible common equity was 44% annualized. Schwab is a savings and loan holding company whose borrowings are part of its funding model alongside bank deposits and client cash, so we judge its balance sheet through capital ratios rather than industrial leverage; on the corrected series, FY25 total debt of $31.0 billion sat below cash and short-term investments. At $100.21 the stock trades at 18.3x trailing earnings and 15.4x on the vendor's forward basis, which lines up with FY26E EPS of $6.49. We value the shares a year out on consensus FY27E EPS of $7.83: the Base holds that current-year multiple, the Bull re-rates to the trailing level, and the Bear has FY27 EPS fall back to FY25's $4.65, as EPS fell in FY23, at the Base multiple. Weighted 20%, 60% and 20%, fair value is $115.33, expected upside 15.1%, bear-case downside 28.5% and reward/risk 0.53x, which derives BUY by a narrow margin; we publish the derived label. Holding the Base multiple is the judgment that decides the call. The Street is constructive, at 18 buy, 3 hold and 1 sell, with a $125.45 consensus target.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: The Charles Schwab Corporation (SCHW), founded in 1971 and headquartered in Westlake, Texas, is a savings and loan holding company providing wealth management, securities brokerage, banking, asset management, custody, and financial advisory services. Its principal subsidiaries are the broker-dealer Charles Schwab & Co., Inc., the banking entity Charles Schwab Bank, SSB, and Charles Schwab Investment Management, Inc., the investment advisor for Schwab Funds and Schwab ETFs. The company serves clients through two segments: Investor Services, for individual investors and for retirement plan and business clients, and Advisor Services, for independent registered investment advisors, independent retirement advisors and recordkeepers. At June 30, 2026 it held $13.08 trillion in client assets across 39.8 million active brokerage accounts. Revenue comes from four main lines: net interest revenue, asset management and administration fees, trading revenue and bank deposit account fees. Management estimates that U.S. investable wealth exceeds $90 trillion, which frames the client-asset base as a share of a larger pool.

thesis.body: Schwab turns asset gathering into earnings growth at high returns. Client assets feed every revenue line at once, and in the second quarter revenue grew well ahead of expenses, so the GAAP pre-tax profit margin reached 51.9%. The weak point is the funding model: net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees depend on client cash and the rate path, and FY23 showed how fast earnings can fall when clients move cash. Valued a year out on consensus FY27E EPS, the shares derive BUY by a narrow margin, and the call rests on whether today's forward multiple holds.

catalysts: Asset gathering: second-quarter core net new assets rose 49% year-over-year, the input that drives every revenue line (Growth).
Net interest margin expanded 12 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.00%; further expansion would lift net interest revenue.
Client engagement: daily average trades of 11.9 million and margin loan balances of $165.1 billion support trading revenue and net interest revenue.
Capital return: Schwab repurchased 11.2 million shares for $1.0 billion in the second quarter (Management).
New offerings: Schwab Crypto and the integration of Forge Global Holdings, Inc. extend the platform into digital assets and private markets.
risks: Client cash sorting: a shift of client cash into higher-yielding alternatives, as in 2022 and 2023, would raise funding costs and cut income.
Rate direction: a decline in rates may pressure net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees.
Equity drawdown: falling markets would cut asset-based fees, margin lending and trading activity together.
2023 IDA agreement: minimum and maximum balance commitments with the TD Depository Institutions limit how Schwab can respond to rate changes.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter total net revenues were $7,072 million, up 21% year-over-year, and first-half net revenues were $13,554 million, up 18%. Net interest revenue rose 19% to $3,357 million, asset management and administration fees rose 16% to $1,825 million, trading revenue rose 28% to $1,215 million and bank deposit account fees rose 35% to $333 million. Total expenses excluding interest rose 12% to $3,403 million, so income before taxes rose 31% to $3,669 million and the GAAP pre-tax profit margin reached 51.9%, from 47.9% a year earlier. Net income was $2,800 million, up 32%, and diluted EPS was $1.54, up 43%; adjusted diluted EPS, which excludes $170 million of pre-tax transaction-related costs, was $1.62. EPS grew faster than net income, helped by a lower share count and lower preferred dividends (Management). Return on average common stockholders' equity was 25% annualized. Over five years, net revenue fell 9.3% in FY23 before rising to $23.9 billion in FY25, up 22.0%, while diluted EPS went from $3.50 in FY22 to $2.54 in FY23 and $4.65 in FY25. Quarterly diluted EPS has risen in each of the last four quarters, from $1.08 in the second quarter of 2025 to $1.26, $1.33 and $1.37 before this quarter's figure. The FY26E consensus of $6.49 needs second-half EPS above first-half EPS of $2.91, which assumes those sequential gains continue. Schwab reports no gross-margin, operating-income or EBITDA line, so we read the pre-tax margin and returns on equity instead.
financials.balanceCommentary: Schwab's balance sheet is a bank and broker's, and its borrowings are part of the funding model rather than industrial leverage. Total assets were $517.3 billion at June 30, 2026, up 13% year-over-year, funded mainly by bank deposits of $249.7 billion and payables to brokerage clients of $124.0 billion; client transactional sweep cash ended June at $485.7 billion. Stockholders' equity was $50.1 billion. This edition uses a corrected FY25 debt series built from the balance-sheet borrowing lines. Total debt was $31.0 billion, matching the year-end long-term debt of $22.2 billion, other short-term borrowings of $6.9 billion and Federal Home Loan Bank borrowings of $1.9 billion. Cash and short-term investments of $46.0 billion exceeded it, for FY25 net debt of -$15.1 billion. The debt series peaked at $59.1 billion in FY23; the 10-K says that in 2022 and 2023 the company extensively utilized higher-cost funding sources as clients moved cash out of sweep, and the series has fallen in each year since. At June 30, 2026 long-term debt was $22.7 billion, which includes a liability for a multi-year software license, other short-term borrowings were $13.9 billion, up 64% year-over-year, and Federal Home Loan Bank borrowings were $0.5 billion. Net debt/EBITDA and interest coverage are blank because there is no EBITDA or operating-income line; for a bank the capital test is the leverage ratio. The consolidated Tier 1 leverage ratio was 8.7% and the adjusted Tier 1 leverage ratio 6.8%, down from 9.8% and 7.2% a year earlier. That decline is the counterpoint to the net-cash reading: capital remains sound but is thinner than a year ago, while bank loans grew 33% to $67.0 billion.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Reported operating cash flow for a bank and broker swings with balance-sheet flows rather than tracking earnings: it was $19.6 billion in FY23, $2.7 billion in FY24 and $9.3 billion in FY25. The FY25 free cash flow of $8.8 billion and the 6.2% FCF yield therefore do not measure recurring cash generation, and we do not value the shares on them. Capital expenditure was $548 million in FY25, small against net income of $8.9 billion. Second-quarter capital expenditures were $792 million, but $633 million of that related to a multi-year software license with a corresponding liability recognized in long-term debt, so the quarter reflects one licensing item rather than a step-up in recurring spending. FY25 capital return, $7.3 billion of repurchases and $2.3 billion of dividends, ran ahead of reported operating cash flow; for a bank the binding limit on that return is regulatory capital rather than cash flow, which is why the falling Tier 1 leverage ratio set out above matters more than the FCF line.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $100.21 Schwab trades at 18.3x trailing earnings. The vendor labels its 15.4x forward multiple next-twelve-month, but it lines up with the price over FY26E EPS of $6.49, so we treat it as a current-year multiple; on FY27E EPS of $7.83 the stock trades at about 12.8x. We compare multiples on one basis: a year from now FY27 becomes the current year, so the like-for-like reference for a multiple on FY27E is today's current-year multiple, not the FY27E one. Price-to-sales of 6.7x carries little meaning when the top line is net revenue, and the EV/EBITDA cell is empty because Schwab reports no EBITDA. The price sits below the 52-week high of $114.53 and above the low of $83.96 even though EPS has risen every quarter, so the trailing multiple has compressed over the year; the pack carries no price history that explains the move. The case for holding the current-year multiple: return on tangible common equity of 44%, a GAAP pre-tax profit margin of 51.9%, and a consensus target of $125.45 (median $125.50) that sits above the value it gives. The case against: consensus EPS growth from FY26E to FY27E is slower than from FY25 to FY26E, the second quarter combined daily average trades up 57% with a net interest margin that a falling-rate year could reverse, and the FY26E estimate needs a stronger second half. We hold the multiple, and that choice decides the label. Of 22 analysts, 18 rate the stock Buy, 3 Hold and 1 Sell, with targets from $91.00 to $145.00. The dividend yield is 1.28%.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Asset gathering and client engagement stay near second-quarter levels, net interest margin keeps expanding from 3.00% and estimates hold or rise. The market then pays for consensus FY27E EPS the 18.3x it pays today for trailing earnings, a re-rating from today's current-year multiple. That prices the shares near the top of the Street's target range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Client assets compound near the current pace and EPS tracks consensus to FY27E $7.83. The forward multiple holds at today's 15.4x current-year level, so the return is consensus earnings growth with no re-rating. The consensus target of $125.45 sits a little above this value.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Rates fall or clients move cash into higher-yielding alternatives, and an equity drawdown cuts asset-based fees, margin lending and trading. FY27 EPS falls back to FY25's $4.65, a reversal of the kind FY23 showed when diluted EPS fell from $3.50 to $2.54. The multiple holds at the Base level, so the downside comes from earnings; we make no further cut for borrowings, which a P/E-based price already nets out. The price sits below the 52-week low and below every Street target.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base at 60% and the Bull and Bear at 20% each. The Bull needs a re-rating the market has not granted this year, since the trailing multiple fell while EPS rose. The Bear's weight rests on its own story: one of the four year-over-year EPS changes in the five-year table was a decline of this kind, in FY23, but the second quarter shows none of its conditions yet, with the federal funds target unchanged through June, net interest margin rising and sweep cash up $24.2 billion from the prior quarter-end, so we set the weight below that one-in-four rate. The weighted fair value is $115.33, an expected upside of 15.1%, against a bear-case downside of 28.5%, for reward/risk of 0.53x. That derives BUY, and we publish the derived label without the one-notch-conservative option. The call is close: reward/risk sits just above the 0.50x BUY line, so the Base multiple decides it. A Base multiple only a fraction of a turn lower, or five points of weight moved from Bull to Bear, derives HOLD; a Base at the consensus target instead would raise expected upside and still derive BUY. Our $113-$128 target range spans the Base at one turn of multiple either side of the Base multiple on FY27E EPS.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor shows a single reportable segment, while the 10-Q describes two, Investor Services and Advisor Services; we follow the 10-Q, but the pack carries no split between them, so FY25 net revenue of $23.9 billion appears as one consolidated total. Net interest revenue, at $3,357 million in the second quarter, was earned on average interest-earning assets of $445.0 billion in the second quarter. Asset management and administration fees track client assets, $6,671.7 billion of which received ongoing advisory services at June 30, 2026. Trading revenue rose with client activity even as revenue per trade fell to $1.64 from $2.03 a year earlier. Bank deposit account fees come from cash swept to the TD Depository Institutions under the 2023 IDA agreement. The mix spreads the business across rate, asset and activity drivers, but net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees both depend on client cash.

moatFactors.name: Scale
moatFactors.body: Schwab held $13.08 trillion in client assets at June 30, 2026. Scale spreads technology and compliance costs across that base: expenses excluding interest were 0.11% of average client assets in the second quarter, against 0.12% a year earlier.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs and custody
moatFactors.body: Custody, advisory and banking relationships are costly to move for clients and for independent advisors. The base is gaining assets rather than losing them: core net new assets rose 49% in the second quarter even as off-platform brokered CDs saw net outflows of $1.1 billion.

moatFactors.name: Diversified revenue model
moatFactors.body: Every revenue line grew double digits in the second quarter (Financials), and the lines respond to different drivers: rates for net interest revenue, asset levels for fees, and activity for trading. That spread lets results hold across environments better than any single line could.

moatFactors.name: Cost efficiency
moatFactors.body: Second-quarter expenses excluding interest grew 12% against revenue growth of 21%, operating leverage that follows from the low cost per dollar of client assets noted above. We rate it Moderate because expense growth still ran in double digits.

businessMoat.durability: The scale and custody advantages look durable: client assets and advisory balances keep growing, and the cost of moving custodied assets protects the base. The main threat is less competitive displacement than the rate cycle, which can compress the rate-sensitive lines even while assets grow, as FY23 showed (Risks). The moat is wide, but the earnings it produces are cyclical, which is why the Bear prices a reversal of that kind rather than a loss of franchise.

points: Asset gathering: core net new assets were $119.8 billion in the second quarter, up 49%, and $259.8 billion for the six months, up 19%; June's $62.7 billion was an annualized organic growth rate of 5.8%.
Client assets reached $13.08 trillion at June 30, 2026, up 22% year-over-year, supported by equity market growth as well as asset gathering, so part of the rise would reverse in a market decline.
Accounts: 1.4 million new brokerage accounts in the quarter, up 26%, brought active brokerage accounts to 39.8 million, up 6% year-over-year.
Lending: bank loan balances were $67.0 billion at June month-end, up 33% year-over-year, and Pledged Asset Line balances were $33.4 billion, up 59% from 2Q25.

Consensus expects revenue of $28.3 billion in FY26E and $31.7 billion in FY27E, from $23.9 billion in FY25, with EPS of $6.49 and $7.83. The counterweight is that the second quarter's trading activity and strong markets set a high base for those estimates.

New products: Schwab Crypto offers Bitcoin and Ethereum trading to retail clients, and the 10-Q lists the integration of Forge Global Holdings, Inc. and its private market capabilities among its forward-looking items; neither is yet a disclosed revenue line.

management.leadership: Richard A. Wurster is President and Chief Executive Officer and Michael D. Verdeschi is Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer, per the 2026 proxy statement (titles as of December 31, 2025); the July 21, 2026 earnings release quotes both in those roles. Walter W. Bettinger II and Charles R. Schwab are Co-Chairmen of the Board, and Jonathan M. Craig is Managing Director and Head of Investor Services. The proxy reports 2025 results under this team: net revenue of $23.9 billion, up 22%, diluted EPS of $4.65, up 56%, ROCE of 21% and ROTCE of 38%, with core net new assets of $519.4 billion, up 42%. The first half of 2026 extends that record, consistent with management's stated strategy of coupling scale with expense discipline.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital return runs through buybacks, a rising dividend and management of the preferred stack. In FY25 Schwab repurchased $7.3 billion of stock and paid $2.3 billion of dividends. In the second quarter of 2026 it repurchased 11.2 million shares for $1.0 billion, and dividends declared were $.32 per share, matching the prior quarter, up 19% from $.27 a year earlier. It redeemed $2.1 billion of Series I Preferred Stock and issued $1.5 billion of Series L Preferred Stock, and preferred stock dividends and other fell to $119 million from $149 million. The diluted share count fell to 1,739 million from 1,822 million a year earlier. The trade-off is capital: the consolidated Tier 1 leverage ratio fell over the year (Financials), so buybacks compete with growth in bank loans and margin lending for the same capital. We view the current pace as appropriate while returns on tangible equity stay near second-quarter levels.
management.governance: Governance rests on the 2026 proxy statement, filed April 6, 2026. At that date the board had 14 directors, and the proxy said the number would fall by one at the annual meeting because Ms. Martin-Flickinger was not standing for re-election. Directors serve staggered three-year terms in three classes, which slows board turnover. The board determined every director independent under NYSE standards except Mr. Schwab, Mr. Bettinger, Mr. Wurster and Ms. Schwab-Pomerantz, so both Co-Chairmen are non-independent. Some directors and their affiliates have ordinary-course credit transactions with Schwab's banking and brokerage subsidiaries on substantially the same terms as for unrelated persons. On February 12, 2025, TD Bank sold 133.8 million voting and 31.7 million non-voting shares in a resale offering, and Schwab repurchased 19.2 million further non-voting shares from it; TD Bank no longer beneficially owns 5%, and the stockholder agreement with it was terminated that day. For outside holders, the end of that agreement removes a large holder's board designation and voting arrangements, while the staggered board and two non-independent Co-Chairmen keep influence with insiders.
management.insiderOwnership: Ownership is reported as of March 3, 2026. Charles R. Schwab beneficially owns 103,039,913 shares, or 5.9%, including shares held by trusts, family limited partnerships and nonprofit public benefit corporations, for the last of which he disclaims beneficial ownership. Directors and executive officers as a group (21 persons) own 110,047,278 shares, or 6.3%. BlackRock, Inc. is listed at 96,697,577 shares, or 5.6%, based on a Schedule 13G/A filed January 31, 2024, so that figure is dated. No holder approaches control; Mr. Schwab's stake aligns him with outside holders without giving him a controlling position.

idiosyncratic: Client cash sorting: the 10-K calls client cash balances a significant funding source for revenue. In 2022 and 2023 rapid rate increases drove clients out of sweep cash into higher-yielding alternatives, and the company extensively utilized higher-cost funding sources, which negatively impacted net income. Client cash was 9.0% of client assets at June 30, 2026, down from 9.9% a year earlier, so the risk remains live even though sweep cash rose in the quarter.

Interest-rate direction: a decline in rates may reduce net interest revenue and bank deposit account fee revenue if asset yields fall more than funding costs or if mortgage prepayments increase; a rise may push funding costs up if competition induces Schwab to raise deposit rates or replace deposits with higher-cost funding sources, as it did in recent years.

2023 IDA agreement: fees on cash swept to the TD Depository Institutions carry prescribed minimum and maximum balance commitments that limit Schwab's ability to respond to rate changes, and the fee revenue may be less than the net interest revenue the deposits could have earned internally.

Securities-portfolio marks: held-to-maturity securities of $130.6 billion and available-for-sale securities of $62.5 billion at June 30, 2026 are exposed to rate moves. The 10-K says the 2022 and 2023 rate increases contributed to increased unrealized losses, and that such losses can reduce market or client confidence.
risks.systemic: Schwab's results move with the economy and markets. General economic, market and geopolitical conditions drive client asset valuations, trading activity and interest rates, all outside the company's control. Federal Reserve monetary policy has a significant effect on net interest revenue, bank deposit account fees and the market value of the investment portfolio; the Fed kept its target rate unchanged through the six months ended June 30, 2026, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 25 basis points to 4.44% over that period. Equity-market declines reduce asset-based fees, margin demand and trading at the same time. As an interconnected financial institution, Schwab is also exposed to problems at other financial institutions, which can reduce available liquidity, raise borrowing and capital costs, and harm confidence in Schwab even without direct exposure. These forces amplify the company's rate and cash-allocation sensitivities rather than adding a separate risk.

body: We rate Schwab BUY with a $113-$128 target range around a Base of $120.58. The second quarter showed client assets, revenue and EPS all growing at double-digit rates with a pre-tax margin above half of revenue, and the corrected FY25 balance sheet shows borrowings below cash and short-term investments, with capital judged by a Tier 1 leverage ratio that is sound but lower than a year ago. Weighted 20%, 60% and 20%, the scenarios give fair value of $115.33, expected upside of 15.1% and reward/risk of 0.53x, which derives BUY; we publish the derived label.

The BUY is narrow, and we say so. It holds because we keep today's 15.4x current-year multiple on FY27E EPS; a lower Base multiple or a heavier Bear derives HOLD, as set out under Valuation. The Bear at $71.61 prices an FY23-style earnings reversal and sits below every Street target.

On the page's own math, a close only slightly above $100.21 pulls reward/risk under 0.50x and derives HOLD, while a close in the low nineties, still above the lowest Street target of $91.00, derives STRONG BUY. We would move to HOLD on a quarter in which core net new assets or net interest margin fall from second-quarter levels, since either would undercut the consensus EPS the Base relies on.
